title: Load balancer: share the work, skip the dead
intro: Three servers sit behind one balancer. Watch where each request goes, and what happens when one server dies.

predict.question: Server 2 has crashed. Where does the next request, which would normally go to Server 2, get sent?
options: Server 2, and the user sees an error
Server 3, because the balancer skips the dead server
Server 1, and the balancer restarts the rotation
predict.reveal: The health check found Server 2 dead, so the balancer removes it from rotation and the turn passes to the next healthy server, Server 3.

takeaway: A load balancer spreads requests across servers and uses health checks to stop sending traffic to any server that fails.

steps.say: Your food app is busy. One balancer stands in front of three identical servers and hands out incoming requests.
Request 1 arrives. Round robin means taking turns in order, so it goes to Server 1.
Request 2 goes to Server 2. Nobody is overloaded yet.
Request 3 goes to Server 3. Everyone has done one job.
Request 4 wraps back to Server 1. The load is shared evenly with no clever math.
Uh-oh: Server 2 crashes. The balancer has not noticed yet.
The balancer sends a health check, a tiny 'are you alive?' ping, every few seconds. Server 2 stays silent.
Request 5 would have been Server 2's turn. The balancer skips it and sends it to Server 3 instead.
Request 6 goes to Server 1. Users never see an error, just two servers sharing the work.
Server 2 is repaired and answers the next ping, so the balancer adds it back into rotation.
Health checks make failures invisible to users: traffic simply flows around the dead server.
